newsitem.title: USA: U.S. factories busiest in 1-1/2 years in May.
newsitem.headline: U.S. factories busiest in 1-1/2 years in May.

text.p: A rebound in auto manufacturing helped push U.S. industrial output up in May as the nation's mines, factories and utilities ran at their fastest clip in more than 1-1/2 years, the Federal Reserve said on Tuesday.

Industrial production climbed 0.4 percent last month after a revised 0.3 percent gain in April, boosting capacity use last month to 83.7 percent from 83.6 percent in April -- the highest use rate since 83.9 percent in September 1995. The rise in output was significantly higher than the 0.2 percent gain forecast by Wall Street economists and was likely to fan inflation concerns as it showed businesses running nearer their production limits.
The Fed said that a partial rebound in automaking bolstered industrial output in May. A strike against industry leader General Motors Corp. ended during the month.
The assembly rate for new cars rose to 5.8 million a year in May from 5.7 million in April and for light trucks it was up to 5.4 million from 5.3 million.
"Continued strength in commercial aircraft and the high-technology sector also contributed to the widespread gains among durable manufacturing industries," the Fed said.
Mining production increased 2 percent in May, partly because electrical utilities were restocking their inventories of coal, after falling 0.5 percent in April.
But utilities output dropped 1.9 percent following a 2.3 percent jump in April, in part becasue relatively cool weather reduced the need for air conditioning.

Analysts said the industrial production report showed the economy was slowing only gradually from its exceptionally brisk first-quarter rate of growth and some said it was displaying troubling hints of potential price pressures.

"We're looking at a slowdown in the second quarter, obviously, but this still seems to suggest there's some underlying momentum," said economist Rick Egelton of Harris Bank/Bank of Montreal of Montreal.
"We're still getting high levels of capacity utilization, so I think the threat on the price side in the future is still there," he added.

During May, manufacturing industries increased their production by 0.5 percent after a 0.2 percent increase in April. It was the strongest monthly pickup in manufacturing output since a 0.6 percent rise in February.
Previously, the Fed said that April industrial outpout was unchanged and that March production was up 0.6 percent, but it revised both estimates.

Economist Raphael Marrone of Deutsche Morgan Grenfell Inc. in New York said strong manufacturing was consistent with overall economic growth in the range of 2-3/4 percent to 3 percent during the second quarter.

Gross domestic product, the broadest measure of overall economic activity, soared at a 5.8 percent annual rate in the first three months of this year but is expected to slow as consumers rein in spending that fuelled the first-quarter surge.
